summary: Linear search checks elements one by one from the start until it finds the target or runs out. It needs no ordering and no random access, so it works on unsorted arrays and linked lists, at O(n) cost.

sections.heading: Algorithm
bullets: Compare the element with the target.
Otherwise advance; if the end is reached, return -1.

sections.heading: Complexity
bullets: Best case: O(1), target is first.
Worst: n comparisons, O(n): target last or absent.

sections.heading: When to use it
bullets: Unsorted or small data, where sorting first would cost more.
Linked lists and streams, which allow only sequential access.
A single search on data you will not search again.
When simplicity matters more than speed.

sections.heading: Sentinel optimization
sections.body: Put the target at the end of the array as a sentinel so the loop needs only one comparison per element (no index bound check). Afterward, restore the last element and decide whether the match was real.
Do not return on the first match; record every index (or count). Time stays O(n).
If some items are searched far more often, moving a found item toward the front makes future searches cheaper. Effective on skewed access patterns such as caches of recent keys.

Binary search is O(log n) but requires sorted data with random access. If you search once, linear search is cheaper than sorting (O(n log n)) plus binary search. If you search many times, sort once and use binary search or a hash table.
If the data is sorted ascending, stop as soon as an element exceeds the target. This halves the average cost for absent targets but is still O(n).

takeaways: Check each element in order: O(n) time, O(1) space.
Works on unsorted data and linked lists.
Best for small or one-off searches.
